title: Sexual Harassment in the Workplace
blurb: What sexual harassment looks like, who it can come from including guests, and what staff and the venue must do about it.
siteNotes: Who to report to on each shift, including late at night at events and weddings
Where the venue's sexual harassment policy and risk assessment are kept
What a manager does when a guest is the problem (for example speaking to the guest, moving them, or asking them to leave)
legalNotes: From BHB-10MT-25. Sexual harassment: Equality Act 2010, section 26. Employer duty to take reasonable steps to prevent it: Equality Act 2010, section 40A, in force from 26 October 2024.

CHECK: the trainer says employers must take "reasonable steps" to prevent sexual harassment, including by guests. From October 2026 the Employment Rights Act 2025 is expected to raise this to "all reasonable steps" and to strengthen protection for harassment by third parties. Confirm the wording and the date before the session is relied on.

CHECK: the trainer says no one will be victimised for raising a genuine concern (Equality Act 2010, section 27). Confirm the venue has a written policy, a named person to report to and a record of the steps it takes.

cards.title: Sexual Harassment in the Workplace
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- recognise sexual harassment, from anyone
- know that guests are no exception
- report it and expect support

cards.title: Never acceptable
cards.body: Sexual harassment is unwanted conduct of a sexual nature, and it is never acceptable at Black Horse Beamish. In hospitality, with late nights, alcohol and lots of social contact, everyone needs to know where the line is and that they will be supported if it is crossed.

cards.title: A wide range of behaviour
cards.body: It covers a wide range of behaviour. None of it is "just banter".

cards.title: Anyone, guests included
cards.body: It can come from a colleague, a manager, a supplier or a guest, and none of those is an exception. A customer being "a bit handsy" is not just part of the job.

right.title: Is never
items: Worth keeping quiet for an easy life

cards.title: We have to act
cards.body:
The law now places a positive duty on employers to take reasonable steps to prevent sexual harassment, including by third parties such as guests. We actively look out for it and act on it.
> Your comfort and safety matter more than avoiding an awkward moment.

cards.title: Tell a manager
cards.body:
If it happens to you, or you see it happening to someone else, report it to a manager. You will be listened to and supported, and no one will be victimised for raising a genuine concern. If a guest is the problem, tell a manager rather than handling it alone.
> We would far rather lose a booking than let a colleague be harassed.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Sexual harassment is unwanted conduct of a sexual nature. It is never acceptable.
- Comments, "jokes", touching, leering, messages, rumours and advances all count.
- It can come from a colleague, manager, supplier or guest.
- Employers must take reasonable steps to prevent it, including by guests.
- Report it to a manager. Do not handle a guest alone.

options: Any friendly comment about someone's appearance
Only touching that leaves an injury
Unwanted conduct of a sexual nature
cards.why: Sexual harassment is unwanted conduct of a sexual nature. It is never acceptable.

cards.q: Sexual harassment can come from a guest, not just a colleague.
cards.why: It can come from a colleague, manager, supplier or guest, and none of those is an exception.

cards.q: A customer being "a bit handsy" is…
options: Not acceptable, so tell a manager
Fine if they are a regular
cards.why: It is not part of the job. Tell a manager.

cards.q: Employers now have a duty to take reasonable steps to prevent sexual harassment.
cards.why: The law places a positive duty on employers to take reasonable steps, including against harassment by third parties such as guests.

cards.q: If it happens to you, you should…
options: Wait and see if it stops
cards.why: Report it to a manager. You will be listened to and supported.

cards.q: Unwanted sexual "jokes" can be a form of sexual harassment.
cards.why: Sexual comments or "jokes" are on the list of behaviour that can be sexual harassment.

cards.q: If a guest is harassing a colleague, what should you do rather than handle it alone?
options: Wait for the colleague to complain
Ignore it until it happens again
cards.why: Tell a manager rather than trying to handle it alone.

cards.q: Someone who reports a genuine concern will be victimised.
cards.why: No one will be victimised for raising a genuine concern.

cards.q: Whether conduct is "unwanted" is judged mainly by…
cards.why: It is about how the conduct is experienced by the person on the receiving end.

cards.q: We would rather lose a booking than let a colleague be harassed.
cards.why: Your comfort and safety matter more than a booking or an awkward moment.
